_note: SYNTHETIC demo data (spec 23). These examiner feedback forms were written for the hackathon demo from each module's public description and learning outcomes in modules.raw.json. They are not real Imperial exam papers or examiner reports. Seeded into exam_forms by seedIfEmpty when no forms exist.

questions.label: Q1: Dimensional analysis and similarity
questions.whatGoodAnswersDid: Good answers listed the variables first, chose repeating variables that span the dimensions, and checked each group was dimensionless before using it to scale the model test.
commonMistakes: Choosing a repeating variable that is itself dimensionless, which leaves too few groups
Assuming complete similarity when the Reynolds and Froude numbers cannot both be matched
revisionPointers: Rework the Buckingham Pi examples from the lecture notes, writing the dimension matrix every time
Revise complete and incomplete similarity, and practise saying which group a wind-tunnel test can actually match

questions.label: Q2: Navier-Stokes and exact solutions (Couette-Poiseuille flow)
questions.whatGoodAnswersDid: Good answers stated each simplifying assumption (steady, fully developed, incompressible) before cancelling terms, and applied the no-slip condition on both walls.
commonMistakes: Cancelling the pressure-gradient term in a pressure-driven flow
Applying only one boundary condition and leaving an integration constant undetermined
revisionPointers: Practise reducing the Navier-Stokes equations term by term for channel and pipe flows
Check every velocity profile against the boundary conditions before computing the shear stress

questions.label: Q3: Boundary layers and the Blasius solution
questions.whatGoodAnswersDid: Good answers used the order-of-magnitude argument to justify the boundary-layer equations, then used the Blasius result for the thickness and the skin-friction drag on the plate.
commonMistakes: Confusing the boundary-layer thickness with the displacement thickness
Using the laminar Blasius result beyond the transition Reynolds number
Forgetting to integrate the wall shear stress over the plate length to get the drag force
revisionPointers: Revise the derivation of the boundary-layer equations from the scaling argument in the notes
Work through the flat-plate drag tutorial problems, laminar first and then turbulent
Make a one-page summary of the thickness definitions (99%, displacement, momentum) with when to use each

questions.label: Q4: Turbulent pipe flow and the time-averaged equations (RANS)
questions.whatGoodAnswersDid: Good answers explained where the Reynolds stresses come from in the averaging, and used the Moody chart with a correctly computed relative roughness.
commonMistakes: Treating the Reynolds stress as a molecular viscous stress
Reading the Moody chart with the wrong Reynolds number or roughness ratio
revisionPointers: Rederive the Reynolds-averaged momentum equation once without notes
Practise head-loss problems with the Moody chart until the iteration feels routine

questions.label: Q5: Compressible flow in converging-diverging nozzles
questions.whatGoodAnswersDid: Good answers identified whether the nozzle was choked, used the isentropic relations from the throat, and checked the exit Mach number against the back pressure.
commonMistakes: Using the isentropic relations across a normal shock
Not checking whether the throat is choked before computing the mass flow
revisionPointers: Revise the area-Mach number relation and when the throat chokes
Sketch the pressure distribution along the nozzle for falling back pressures

forms.generalComments: Synthetic demo form. Most of the cohort did well on the integral and dimensional questions. Marks were mostly lost where approximations had to be justified rather than applied, especially in the boundary-layer question.

questions.label: Q1: Gas turbine (Brayton) cycle analysis
questions.whatGoodAnswersDid: Good answers drew the T-s diagram first, used isentropic efficiencies for the compressor and turbine, and found the work ratio and thermal efficiency.
commonMistakes: Applying an isentropic efficiency the wrong way round for the compressor
Using the cold-air standard specific heats when the question gave temperature-dependent data
revisionPointers: Practise drawing the T-s diagram before writing any equations
Revise the definitions of compressor and turbine isentropic efficiency side by side

questions.label: Q2: Steam plant (Rankine cycle) with reheat
questions.whatGoodAnswersDid: Good answers read the steam tables carefully, interpolated where needed, and checked the dryness fraction at the turbine exit.
commonMistakes: Reading saturated-liquid values where superheated values were needed
Forgetting the feed-pump work when computing the net work
revisionPointers: Work through two reheat cycle problems end to end with the steam tables
Always state the state point table (p, T, h, s, x) before computing efficiencies

questions.label: Q3: Refrigeration and psychrometry
questions.whatGoodAnswersDid: Good answers used the psychrometric chart to track each process and stated the coefficient of performance with the right definition.
commonMistakes: Mixing up the heat pump and refrigerator definitions of the coefficient of performance
Ignoring the condensate leaving the cooling coil
revisionPointers: Revise the vapour-compression cycle on the p-h diagram
Practise air-conditioning processes on the psychrometric chart

questions.label: Q4: Heat exchanger selection and performance
questions.whatGoodAnswersDid: Good answers chose between the LMTD and effectiveness-NTU methods based on what was known, and commented on the economic and material constraints.
commonMistakes: Using the LMTD method when the outlet temperatures were unknown
Not discussing practical constraints when asked to justify a design
revisionPointers: Revise when to use LMTD and when to use effectiveness-NTU
Practise short written justifications that mention materials, cost and the environment

forms.generalComments: Synthetic demo form. Cycle analysis was generally strong. Written justification of design choices was the weakest area across the cohort.

questions.label: Q1: Stress transformation and Mohr's circle
questions.whatGoodAnswersDid: Good answers drew Mohr's circle to scale, labelled the plane angles, and found the principal stresses and maximum shear stress.
commonMistakes: Using the physical angle rather than twice the angle on Mohr's circle
Sign errors in the shear stress convention
revisionPointers: Practise Mohr's circle questions with a fixed sign convention written at the top of the page
Check principal stresses with the transformation equations as well as the circle

questions.label: Q2: Failure criteria for ductile and brittle materials
questions.whatGoodAnswersDid: Good answers chose Tresca or von Mises for the ductile case and maximum principal stress for the brittle case, and quoted a safety factor.
commonMistakes: Applying a ductile criterion to a brittle material
Leaving out the safety factor when asked whether a design is safe
revisionPointers: Make a table of the failure criteria with when each applies
Revise safety factors with one worked design check per criterion

questions.label: Q3: Thick-walled cylinders (Lamé equations)
questions.whatGoodAnswersDid: Good answers applied the boundary conditions at both radii and identified the bore as the critical location.
commonMistakes: Applying thin-walled formulae to a thick cylinder
Using the wrong boundary condition at the outer radius
revisionPointers: Rework the Lamé derivation and the compound cylinder example
Practise identifying where the maximum hoop stress occurs

questions.label: Q4: Plastic bending and residual stresses in beams
questions.whatGoodAnswersDid: Good answers sketched the stress distribution at each stage and found the residual stresses by superposing the elastic unloading.
commonMistakes: Forgetting that unloading is elastic
Confusing the shape factor with the safety factor
revisionPointers: Practise the elastic-plastic bending examples, sketching the stress block every time
Revise residual stress by superposition with the tutorial sheet

questions.label: Q5: Euler buckling of struts
questions.whatGoodAnswersDid: Good answers used the right effective length for the end conditions and checked whether the strut yields before it buckles.
commonMistakes: Using the pinned-pinned effective length for every end condition
Not checking yield against buckling for short struts
revisionPointers: Revise the effective length for each set of end conditions
Practise deciding between yield and buckling using the slenderness ratio

forms.generalComments: Synthetic demo form. Mohr's circle and buckling were well answered. Plastic bending and residual stress caused most difficulty.

questions.label: Q1: Separation of variables for 2D PDEs
questions.whatGoodAnswersDid: Good answers set up the eigenvalue problem from the homogeneous boundary conditions first and used orthogonality to find the Fourier coefficients.
commonMistakes: Choosing the wrong sign of the separation constant
Applying the non-homogeneous boundary condition before finding the eigenfunctions
revisionPointers: Rework the Laplace and heat equation examples from the notes
Revise Fourier series coefficients and orthogonality

questions.label: Q2: Finite difference and finite volume schemes
questions.whatGoodAnswersDid: Good answers derived the scheme from a Taylor expansion, stated its order of accuracy, and treated the boundary nodes explicitly.
commonMistakes: Stating the order of accuracy without deriving it
Mixing up the differential and integral forms when building a finite volume scheme
revisionPointers: Derive the central difference stencil and its truncation error from scratch
Practise writing a finite volume balance for one cell

questions.label: Q3: Convergence, consistency and stability
questions.whatGoodAnswersDid: Good answers distinguished consistency from convergence clearly and used the stability condition to choose the time step.
commonMistakes: Treating consistency and convergence as the same thing
Choosing a time step that breaks the stability limit
revisionPointers: Revise the definitions of consistency, stability and convergence with one example each
Practise finding the stability limit for the explicit heat equation scheme

questions.label: Q4: Iterative solution of linear systems in Python
questions.whatGoodAnswersDid: Good answers wrote a clear Jacobi or Gauss-Seidel loop with a residual-based stopping test and commented on convergence.
commonMistakes: Stopping after a fixed number of iterations without checking the residual
Updating the solution in place in a Jacobi loop
revisionPointers: Rewrite the Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel solvers from the computing labs without notes
Practise residual-based stopping tests

forms.generalComments: Synthetic demo form. Analytical questions were strong. Many lost marks on the conceptual question on consistency and convergence.
